summary: This document updates the IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) so tunnel protocols that use UDP over IPv6 can skip the UDP checksum in certain cases. This is allowed when the tunnel's header information is protected on the inner packet being carried. Skipping it avoids the computation cost and improves performance.

plainLanguage.summary: Checking every package twice is slow. If the package inside is already checked, this lets the outer wrapper skip its check.

questions: can ipv6 udp checksum be zero
why do udp tunnels skip the checksum
what does rfc 6935 change in rfc 2460
subtitle: Why IPv6 tunnels over UDP are allowed to send a zero checksum, and the conditions that make it safe enough.

tldr.problem: IPv4 lets UDP skip its checksum, but RFC 2460 says IPv6 receivers must discard UDP packets with a zero checksum. For tunnel endpoints that carry already checksummed packets, computing the outer checksum is seen as an unwarranted burden.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the relevant text of RFC 2460 so a node associates a mode with each UDP port. The default mode keeps the old rule, while certain tunnel protocols may enable zero-checksum mode for specific ports if they follow the node and usage requirements of RFC 6936.
tldr.outcome: UDP tunnels over IPv6 can skip the outer checksum computation. The RFC warns that misdelivery becomes more likely to be accepted, so tunnel protocols must be robust to it.

facts.label: Replacement value for a computed zero

today: RFC 6935 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013; the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 2460 and depends on the requirements in RFC 6936.

sections.title: The Problem with IPv6 and UDP Checksums
sections.content:
Many new protocols are deployed as UDP tunnels because firewalls and other middleboxes make truly new protocol numbers hard to deploy. In such a tunnel, an inner packet is carried inside an outer UDP packet. Tunnel endpoints may be routers or middleboxes aggregating traffic from many users, so computing a checksum on the outer packet looks like an unwarranted burden, especially when the inner packet already has one.

IPv4 has a header checksum, so the outer UDP checksum can be set to zero. IPv6 has no checksum in its header, and RFC 2460 says IPv6 receivers MUST discard UDP packets with a zero checksum. The RFC therefore updates RFC 2460 to let endpoints use a zero UDP checksum in constrained situations, following the applicability statement in RFC 6936. It notes that the idea began with the Automatic Multicast Tunnels (AMT) draft, and that LISP and Softwires also wanted it.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 lets you skip one safety check on a parcel, but IPv6 says you must always do it. That is slow for delivery companies who already check what is inside.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Can Tolerate a Zero Checksum
sections.content:
The RFC analyses what happens if a tunnel packet is corrupted. It says tunnel protocols can be robust if they follow several practices. Tunnel state should be set up with checksummed control messages, since undetected errors there could cause long-lived failures. Keepalives should include datagrams with a zero checksum and with a non-zero checksum, so endpoints notice when a middlebox on the path drops zero-checksum datagrams. Receivers should track context by the 5-tuple of tunneled protocol number, IPv6 source and destination addresses, and UDP source and destination ports, and should try to detect corrupted fragments.

Tunnels also have natural protection. A mis-delivered inner packet may reach an address domain where it is not routable, fail a source address check such as Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding, have the wrong type to be delivered, or fail its own checksum. The RFC says none of this guarantees correctness, but it reduces the risk.

Why only tunnels? Their encapsulating packets do nothing except carry data from ingress to egress, so a corruption commonly affects a single tunneled packet and not established protocol state. General servers that do not know their senders should not use a zero checksum, because the checksum is their first verification that a packet was meant for them. Tunnels of IP packets are generally considered safe because every IPv4 and IPv6 packet has at least one checksum, while tunnels of non-IP packets need further analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel packet is like a plain outer box whose only job is to move the inner parcel. If the box is damaged, usually just that parcel is lost, and the inner parcel has its own checks.

sections.title: The Zero UDP Checksum Update
sections.content:
The RFC deletes the fourth bullet of RFC 2460 section 8.1 and replaces it. Under the new text, an IPv6 node associates a mode with each UDP port it sends or receives on.

  • In the default mode, a sender MUST compute the UDP checksum, changing a computed zero to hex FFFF. Receivers MUST by default discard zero-checksum packets and SHOULD log the error.
  • As an alternative, certain protocols that use UDP as a tunnel encapsulation MAY enable zero-checksum mode for a port or set of ports. Any node doing so MUST follow the node requirements in section 4 of RFC 6936, and the protocol MUST follow its usage requirements in section 5.
  • Middleboxes supporting IPv6 MUST follow requirements 9, 10 and 11 of those usage requirements.

Tunnel protocols that want a zero checksum also need a defined method for the case where a middlebox blocks zero-checksum datagrams on the path. This matters because middleboxes that conform to RFC 2460 are likely to discard them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mailbox now has a setting. Normally it insists on the safety check. A few special mailboxes for tunnels can be set to skip it, if they promise to follow extra rules.

sections.title: Additional Observations
sections.content: The RFC adds three observations. First, no empirical study of corruption probabilities had been done, to the authors' knowledge, since about 2000, and it strongly suggests a new study of the IPv6 header, which could lead to revising the recommendations. Second, a key reason for UDP tunnelling is poor middlebox support for new protocols. If middleboxes supported UDP-Lite (RFC 3828), it would give better protection than this update and would be expected to be preferred for many tunnels. Third, the UDP checksum is also overloaded with protecting the IPv6 header, so protocols that do not use a pseudo-header approach have essentially no protection from misdelivered packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say experts should test again how often packets get damaged, and that a different, better safety check exists if routers learn to support it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A zero checksum makes an attack slightly easier to build, but the RFC argues this is not a significant new vulnerability, since checksums are not a security measure and an attacker can generate them easily. Users of zero checksums should apply all feasible checks and context verification, though these will not stop an intentional attack with the correct information. Source address validation can help keep attackers from injecting traffic into contexts.

There is also a processing risk. Depending on hardware, tunnels with zero checksums and with computed checksums may differ in cost, so a tunnel egress built for many zero-checksum packets could be overloaded by an attacker injecting packets with non-zero checksums, for example in a router's slow path. The RFC suggests protections such as source-address filtering and throttling the amount of non-zero checksum traffic, noting that throttling may affect the tunnel protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the check does not make a thief much stronger, because the check never kept thieves out. But a flood of unusual packets could still jam a tunnel exit.

left.title: Default mode
left.desc: Sender computes the checksum and turns a zero result into FFFF. Receiver discards zero-checksum packets and should log the error.

right.title: Zero-checksum mode
right.desc: Only for certain UDP tunnel protocols on chosen ports. Must follow the RFC 6936 node and usage requirements.
